title: Meaning of life
wiki_lead:
The meaning of life is the concept of an individual's life, human life, or existence in general having an inherent significance or a philosophical point. There is no consensus on the specifics of such a concept, or whether the concept itself even exists in any objective sense. Thinking and discourse on the topic is sought in the English language through questions such as—but not limited to—"What is the meaning of life?", "What is the purpose of existence?", and "Why are we here?". There have been many proposed answers to these questions from many different cultural and ideological backgrounds. The search for life's meaning has produced much philosophical, scientific, theological, and metaphysical speculation throughout history. Different people and cultures believe in different answers to this question. Opinions vary on the usefulness of using time and resources in the pursuit of an answer. Excessive pondering can be indicative of, or lead to, an existential crisis.
The meaning of life can be derived from philosophical and religious contemplation of, and scientific inquiries about, existence, social ties, consciousness, and happiness. Many other issues are also involved, such as symbolic meaning, ontology, value, purpose, ethics, good and evil, free will, the existence of one or multiple gods, conceptions of God, the soul, and the afterlife. Scientific contributions focus primarily on describing related empirical facts about the universe, exploring the context and parameters concerning the "how" of life. Science also studies and can provide recommendations for the pursuit of well-being and a related conception of morality. An alternative, humanistic approach poses the question, "What is the meaning of my life?"

Origin of the expression
The first English use of the expression "meaning of life" appears in Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus (1833–1834), book II chapter IX, "The Everlasting Yea". Our Life is compassed round with Necessity; yet is the meaning of Life itself no other than Freedom, than Voluntary Force: thus have we a warfare; in the beginning, especially, a hard-fought battle.Carlyle may have been inspired by earlier usage of the equivalent German expression der Sinn des Lebens by German Romantic writers Novalis and Friedrich Schlegel. Schlegel was the first to use it in print by way of his novel Lucinde (1799), though Novalis had done so in a 1797–1798 manuscript, in which he wrote: "Only an artist can divine the meaning of life." Additionally, the word lebenssinn, translated as life's meaning, had been used by Goethe in a 1796 letter to Schiller. These authors grappled with the rationalism and materialism of modernity. Carlyle called this the "Torch of Science", which burned "more fiercely than ever" and made religion "all parched away, under the Droughts of practical and spiritual Unbelief", resulting in the "Wilderness" of "the wide World in an Atheistic Century".


Origin of the question

Arthur Schopenhauer was the first to explicitly ask the question, in an essay entitled "Character".Since a man does not alter, and his moral character remains absolutely the same all through his life; since he must play out the part which he has received, without the least deviation from the character; since neither experience, nor philosophy, nor religion can effect any improvement in him, the question arises, What is the meaning of life at all? To what purpose is it played, this farce in which everything that is essential is irrevocably fixed and determined?Questions about the meaning of life, and similar, have been expressed in a broad variety of other ways, including:
What is the meaning of life? What's it all about? Who are we?
Why are we here? What are we here for?
What is the origin of life?
What is the nature of life? What is the nature of reality?
What is the purpose of life? What is the purpose of one's life?
What is the significance of life? (See also #Psychological significance and value in life)

grok_lead: The meaning of life is a central philosophical question that probes the purpose, significance, and value of human existence in the universe, often framed as an inquiry into what, if anything, renders life worthwhile beyond mere survival. There is no single, universally agreed-upon ultimate purpose for humanity on Earth. Philosophical theories such as supernaturalism (meaning derived from supernatural or divine sources), naturalism (meaning derived from the natural world, either subjectively or objectively), and nihilism (no inherent or objective meaning) offer diverse frameworks, alongside perspectives from religion, science, and existentialism. These views are often conflicting, with no consensus on an objective cosmic purpose. Consequently, many conclude that meaning is subjective, self-created by individuals, or absent in a purely physical universe. This distinction is key: while "meaning-in-life" refers to an individual's subjective sense of personal purpose and coherence, the "meaning of life" addresses broader, more universal concerns about the nature of existence itself, as explored by existential philosophers such as SÃ¸ren Kierkegaard, Albert Camus, and Friedrich Nietzsche. In philosophy, the topic has been approached through diverse lenses, including ethics, metaphysics, and existentialism, with thinkers emphasizing transcendence of personal limitations through connections to larger values, relationships, or causes. For instance, Robert Nozick argued that meaning emerges from integrating life's goals into a coherent plan that links the individual to wider contexts, such as objective worth or communal contributions, rather than isolated pursuits. Viktor Frankl's logotherapy further posits the pursuit of meaning as a fundamental human motivation, capable of sustaining individuals amid suffering, as evidenced in psychological studies linking a sense of purpose to improved mental health and resilience. Religious traditions provide varied answers, often tying life's meaning to a transcendent order or divine relationship. In Abrahamic faiths like Christianity, human life gains purpose through obedience to God's will, moral living, and preparation for an afterlife, where actions in this world determine eternal reward. In Islam, life is a preparation for the eternal afterlife, lived in obedience to Allah's laws to achieve paradise. Eastern religions such as Hinduism and Buddhism frame meaning around cycles of rebirth and liberation: in Hinduism, it involves fulfilling dharma (duty) to progress toward moksha (release from reincarnation), while Buddhism centers on ending suffering via the Eightfold Path to achieve nirvana. Across these traditions, religion functions sociologically to offer purpose, foster community, and address existential anxieties about mortality. From a scientific viewpoint, particularly evolutionary biology and psychology, life lacks an inherent cosmic purpose but derives significance through adaptive processes and human cognition. Evolutionary perspectives, as in sociobiology, suggest that behaviors promoting survival and reproductionâsuch as cooperation and altruism âprovide a naturalistic basis for meaning, aligning individual actions with species continuity without invoking supernatural elements. Psychological research reinforces this by showing that a perceived purpose correlates with better physical health, longevity, and emotional well-being, often cultivated through relationships, achievements, and contributions to society. Contemporary interdisciplinary work in evolutionary psychology explores cognitive adaptations that enable humans to respond to environmental challenges, including processes related to deriving meaning from existence. The most important thing in life is subjective and varies by individual and culture. However, large-scale surveys across multiple countries consistently identify family as the most frequently cited source of meaning and fulfillment in life, followed by factors like career, health, and relationships.
